title: Mongolia & Central Asia: Milk Ferments and Their Spirits
attribution: The steppe's defining drinks are fermented from mare's and other animal milk — a lineage unique among the world's alcohols. Documented from ethnographic and dairy-science sources; there is no judging guideline for any of them. Values are typical.

styles.name: Airag / Kumis (айраг / кумыс)
styles.impression: Fermented mare's milk — the national drink of Mongolia and the Central Asian steppe. Sour, fizzy, faintly alcoholic and thin, with a sharp dairy tang.
styles.comments: Both lactic-acid bacteria and yeast work at once, so it is simultaneously soured and lightly alcoholic. A pillar of nomadic nutrition; drunk in large quantities in summer. Kumis is the Turkic/Kazakh name, airag the Mongolian.
styles.ingredients: Raw mare's milk, fermented by a mixed lactic-and-yeast culture in a leather bag (khokhuur) or vat, churned thousands of times to aerate. Mare's milk is uniquely high in the lactose the yeast ferment.

styles.name: Tarasun / Milk-Whey Beers
styles.impression: Regional cow- or yak-milk ferments of Buryatia and the wider steppe, sometimes stronger than airag.
styles.comments: Where mares are scarce, other animals' milk is fermented similarly. Shubat (camel) is prized in Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.
styles.ingredients: Cow, yak or camel milk fermented with mixed cultures; camel-milk shubat is the arid-zone equivalent.

styles.name: Arkhi / Nermel (архи)
styles.impression: Mongolia's distilled milk liquor — airag redistilled in a simple stovetop still into a clear, low-strength, faintly cheesy spirit.
styles.comments: 'Arkhi' is now the general Mongolian word for any liquor, but nermel arkhi ('distilled arkhi') specifically means the traditional milk distillate. Central to hospitality and ritual; the first drops are offered to the sky and hearth.
styles.ingredients: Airag (fermented milk), distilled in a household still (the shar arkhi apparatus) over the hearth, often several times.

styles.name: Boza / Bozo
styles.impression: A thick, sweet-sour fermented cereal drink of Central Asia, the Caucasus and the Balkans — porridge-like, low in alcohol, drunk as food.
styles.comments: Ranges from essentially non-alcoholic (Turkish boza) to mildly alcoholic. One of the oldest cereal ferments, spanning a huge geography.
styles.ingredients: Millet, maize, wheat or other grain, cooked to a gruel and fermented with lactic bacteria and yeast.
